reason: The smallest gain worth acting on, in shares of the better model's score on the kind's evaluations (0 to 1): twice the 5 percent tolerance the tier chooser already allows for benchmark noise, because the evaluations publish no interval in our data.

Cost is weighed heavily (the owner's instruction of 2026-11-11): a step up must show a gain whose value is at least three times the added cost. The full condition is: gain at least the larger of noise_floor and cost_weight x added_cost / value_of_gain.

The added cost of a step is the expected cost of the role's calls: calls per turn or run (frequency class) x (cost of a call on the higher tier's model minus on the lower's), in USD, with the list prices of the models that fill the two tiers in force that day (never a name in code). A call costs input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price + cache write tokens x input price x the cache write multiplier + cache read tokens x input price x the cache read multiplier, with the multipliers from the price registry (a blank multiplier means no discount is assumed). Tokens per call are measured where the repository or this machine holds a measurement (the role row says which) and otherwise an estimated volume class.
The value of a full share of gain, in USD per turn or run, is stated by the stakes class: what putting right a wrong call of that class costs. It is what the added cost is weighed against.
The metric climbs the ladder only as far as quality. Best is never reached by the metric: it is set by a person or by the structure watch (the constraint best_only_on_request_or_watch).

If this rule is wrong it is changed in a new recorded revision row with its date and the reason, with the table recomputed once; it is never retuned to move a role. This metric family was retuned after seeing results three times and that is a recorded weakness.

First form, written 2026-11-11 before any role was computed: threshold = 0.10 x frequency factor (many 2, turn 1, rare 0.5) x price premium (log2 of the list price ratio, at least 1) / stakes factor (call 1, turn 2, structure 4); constraints classification fast only, a response a person reads at least balanced, best only for the structure watch. Its table was computed once and moved seven roles; deep work (the main session) came out as quality.

Revised once on the owner's instruction after the first table was seen. His words: 'cost should be prioritized heavily, but apply my earlier guidance on what each tier represents, also what's used for deep work should depend on the task (and in some cases selection of user)', and 'the reason deep work should not jump to a dearer tier is that it spends many tokens, and the metric should have worked that out by itself without a rule of his'. Changed: (1) the threshold no longer uses frequency factors and a price ratio; it is the larger of the noise floor and cost_weight x expected added cost / value of gain, so the cost of the tokens a role spends decides; (2) the stakes classes became value classes in USD and gained task; (3) frequency became calls per turn or run and each role has a volume (tokens per call), measured where the repository holds a measurement; (4) the constraint deep work balanced was never kept: deep work is four roles by task kind scored by the same rule, and main_session follows the implementation role when the task kind is not known. No further tuning.

Second change on the owner's instruction, made after the second table was seen: the session volume is measured from real recorded sessions instead of derived from toy evaluation cases, cache writes and cache reads are priced at their multipliers of the input price (added columns of the price registry), and the dollar values of a full gain and the cost weight are stated as assumptions with their sensitivity recorded in the metric's disadvantages. No constraint was added and no weight, floor or class value was tuned.

The stakes values (0.05, 1, 10 and 50 USD) and the cost weight 3 have no recorded source: the owner's tier meanings in the records (fast for many or straightforward calls, balanced for turn effect, quality for structure and foundational work) fix their order, not their size. They are assumptions; since revision 4 they govern only the per-call roles, no deep-run role depends on them (pinned by a test).

Today one ladder for every kind: fast, balanced, quality, in this order, each tier filled by the model the tier choice names that day. A kind or a role may later carry its own ladder rows (a ladder row with a kind or role set replaces this one for it, the way a role variant replaces a tier's weights in tier_metrics.csv), so a type of task can have its own tiers.

Calls per turn or run: one half. Fewer than one call per turn or run (on a condition, a schedule, a request, or a deep-work session that not every turn starts).
USD per turn or run for a full share of gain: five cents. An error stays inside the call: a later step, a validator or the call's own metric catches it and a retry puts it right.
One dollar. An error changes what the turn does or says, so the turn is redone or a person is misled. The owner's reason for balanced: a significant downstream effect for the turn.

Fifty dollars. An error persists in records, structure or the design of an arm and is found and redone later. The owner's reason for quality: it affects longer-term structure and foundational tasks.

Classification is fast tier only, always (the owner's hard rule, kept as a recorded constraint): a classification prompt is improved by training on past cases on the fast tier, not by buying a larger model, and the calls are many. An explicit tier from a person does not change it.
Any response a person reads is at least balanced (the owner's rule): a person reads the error directly, so the lowest tier is not allowed for prose a person reads.

Best only where a person asks for it or sets it, plus the structure watch (the owner's rule): the watch is the one small call that guards structural risk, so it runs on the best tier without being asked. The metric never reaches best.

Third change on the owner's instruction, a change of definition for the deep-run roles (listed in the deep_run rows below): they no longer climb the ladder by weighing a measured gain against an assumed dollar value and cost weight. His words: 'metric used to decide deep run model must prioritize low cost by default if user doesn't specify higher (either currently or from earlier guidance on model tiers) (with a model that is good enough to get most tasks done), or if s tier fails to do something sufficiently and planner decides to use a higher tier for a specific reason.' The definition now: (1) default = the cheapest tier whose recorded pass rate on the deep-work cases meets the sufficiency bar (one number, stated once in the sufficiency row with its source); (2) the person may set higher, the current request first, then standing guidance on model tiers, then the default; (3) when the default fails a task (after-run check, stop decision or review) the planner may move that task up one rung with a specific reason that is recorded with the run, never for later tasks. The per-call roles keep the earlier rule and its recorded assumptions. No bar, weight or threshold was chosen after seeing which tier wins.

The definition for every deep-run role (the deep_run rows): the tier of the role is the lowest rung of the ladder whose measured pass rate on the recorded deep-work cases meets the sufficiency bar, which is good enough to get most tasks done at the lowest cost. A rung with no measurement is skipped and the rule says so in the row's evidence: the tier is the cheapest MEASURED rung that meets the bar. When no measured rung meets it, the tier is the rung above the highest measured one, and when nothing is measured the previous tier is kept and the row says so. Prices and the gains of the public evaluations do not enter: the cheapest sufficient rung is cheapest by construction.

The sufficiency bar, stated once: a tier is good enough for deep work when at least 0.66 of its recorded deep-work cases pass. Source: the min-pass-rate=0.66 of the whole stage of metric-delegated-agent-sessions-hard (hubofhubs/the_world/tools/delegated_agent_sessions/metrics.csv), the floor the hub already sets for an arm to count on the hard cases (two of three), fixed before this rule was written; a test pins that this source still says 0.66. It is not tuned here: change it only as a new recorded revision.

The recorded measurement a tier is judged on: for each arm row of the tier (the tier= of its arm name) in the kind hard of arm_standings.json beside delegated_agent_sessions, passed_total over cases_total of its latest pooled row, summed over the arms of the tier (several harnesses run the same cases, so each counts). These are the 27 hard deep-work cases of metric-delegated-agent-sessions-hard, real multi-file repository tasks that take minutes. Only tiers that appear there are measured.
An escalation moves one rung up the ladder (fast to balanced, balanced to quality) and never to best: best is a person's explicit tier or the structure watch.

An escalation needs a specific reason (what the default tier did not do sufficiently on this task), recorded with the run as tier_reason. A blank reason, or one that only repeats the signal, is refused.
An escalation applies to the one task that failed. Nothing is stored: the next task is chosen again from the person's input, standing guidance and the default, so an escalation is never sticky.
The after-run code check says the result is insufficient (the resumed turn of after_check_resume).
The stop decision of Goal Completion says the work is not met and the run cannot continue on this tier.
A review (the review agent or a deep_work_review session) says the result is insufficient.
The tier the person names in the current request (the --tier flag or an explicit ask) wins, for a role whose person_may_set is yes.
